A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RoboMaster research. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support reliable comparison despite changes in formatting and section order.

before.justification: v2 reports original Bridge experiments, user preferences, component ablations, robustness tests, and qualitative generalization results.

after.justification: v3 retains those empirical results and adds simulated robot execution, action-conditioned video validation, prompt robustness, and annotation-success measurements.

M1.justification: The generator, collaborative trajectory representation, object embeddings, motion injector, and loss remain unchanged in Section 3. New Section 4.5 extends the downstream procedure with morphology adaptation and a trained inverse-dynamics component that converts generated videos into executable actions.

E1.justification: v3 adds five RLBench and four SIMPLER simulated execution tasks involving Franka and Google Robot morphologies, plus evaluation with inaccurate subject prompts. Bridge and in-the-wild generation coverage remains; shortening Bridge V2 to Bridge and highlighting the existing 21k curated samples do not establish another dataset.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds TesserAct while retaining IRASim, MotionCtrl, DragAnything, and Tora. The new action-planning comparison evaluates OpenVLA, TesserAct, and Tora, substantially extending comparison to executable policies and a 4D world model. The relocated VBench comparison retains its original comparator set.

E3.justification: New planning protocols specify fixed cameras, adaptation on 1,300 pairs excluding evaluated tasks, inverse-model training on 300 video-action samples per evaluated task, and 100 execution trials per task. v3 also introduces action-conditioned video checks including latent L2 and 10–40% prompt-replacement conditions. The existing Bridge evaluation and training settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v3 adds prompt-error sensitivity analysis (Table 8), validation of inferred actions through action-conditioned video generation (Table 3), and single-object versus multiple-object segmentation failure analysis (Appendix B, Table R11). Existing component, mask-sparsity, and trajectory-perturbation ablations retain their results.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or variability across repeated runs or seeds. The new 100-episode planning evaluation specifies an evaluation sample count, rather than repeated-model-run or uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: v3 adds planning, action-validation, prompt-robustness, segmentation, and TesserAct results; TesserAct's Table 2 FVD is 261.84. Existing Bridge objective metrics, VBench scores, and earlier ablation values are unchanged. RoboMaster's preference changes from 47.33% to 45.16% with an expanded comparator set, so this is not a same-setting decline. Table 4 shows seven wins over Tora across nine tasks, contradicting the text's eight-of-ten statement.

T1.justification: Section 3 retains the mathematical definitions, conditional factorization, embedding equations, and loss. v2's motion-injection Equation 6 becomes inline mathematics in v3, renumbering the loss from Equation 7 to Equation 6. No substantive mathematical revision or new proof appears.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the claimed validation from video quality and trajectory control to state-of-the-art robotic action planning. The introduction also promotes the previously documented 21k Bridge curation to an explicit dataset contribution. The central collaborative-trajectory and object-embedding claims remain.

C2.justification: v3 newly interprets better interaction videos as enabling more reliable inverse-dynamics actions. Appendix B substantially expands the earlier brief limitations: 3D occlusion and annotation burden, segmentation failures requiring manual intervention, contributions of pretrained backbone priors, and unresolved generalization to unseen robot morphologies.

D1.justification: v3 documents robot-adaptation compute, the Cosmos model and fine-tuning recipe, and more explicit trajectory-annotation instructions with four transition cases. Appendix B newly discloses approximately 17,000 automatically acceptable masks plus 4,000 manual reannotations behind the retained 21k dataset; this is additional disclosure, not evidence that Bridge curation changed. The architecture table and project link remain.

R1.justification: v3 adds focused citations and discussion concerning TesserAct, Cosmos2.5, OpenVLA, RLBench, SIMPLER, MOFT, and LoRA, extending positioning toward policy extraction and morphology adaptation. Most existing trajectory-control, camera-control, and control-injection related work remains.

P1.justification: Parts of the abstract and introduction are rewritten, user-interaction explanations are condensed or clarified, and terminology and citation style change. References move before the appendices, VBench moves to Appendix D.1, and planning and limitations receive dedicated sections. Most existing method and experimental prose remains closely matched.

P2.justification: v3 substantially expands and reorganizes displays with new action-validation, planning, prompt-robustness, annotation-case, and segmentation tables. Table 2 gains a row, and VBench moves from Table 3 to Table R12. Figure 5 removes the carrot comparison and reorders the box example; Figure S8 is redrawn. The ICLR layout separates references from retained supplementary figure pages.

improvement.justification: v2's proposed utility for robot learning rested mainly on video-quality and control evaluations. v3 adds simulated task execution, action-validation checks, prompt robustness, and quantified annotation failures, substantially strengthening practical validation and transparency. The new evidence remains qualified by inverse-model training on evaluated tasks, absent uncertainty estimates, and the incorrect eight-of-ten summary of Table 4. These weaknesses limit the stronger claims but do not outweigh the substantial evidential gains.
